issues.legal_issue: The business constituted a joint venture rather than the exclusive proprietary business of one participant.
material_facts: The evidence showed that money was advanced toward the business and that land for it was purchased in the names of two participants, after which the poultry business was started.
The business was carried on by the participants, and the Court was satisfied on the record that it was a joint venture, despite the absence of a written partnership document.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the business was a joint venture and not the exclusive proprietary concern of one participant.
issues.legal_principle: Whether the enterprise was a joint venture was determined as a question of fact on the evidence before the Court; the Court found the evidence sufficient to reject the claim that it was solely one participant’s business.

predicates.shared_enterprise_claimed: A party claims that an enterprise was carried on jointly rather than solely by another participant.
predicates.joint_financing_shown: The evidence shows that more than one participant provided or advanced money toward the enterprise.
predicates.jointly_acquired_business_property_shown: Property for the enterprise was acquired in the names of more than one participant.

issues.definition: When a claimed shared enterprise is supported by evidence of joint financing or jointly acquired business property, the enterprise is treated as a joint venture.

issues.legal_issue: An admitted document concerning business accounts must be considered as evidence relevant to whether accounts were finally settled and whether a claim is time-barred.
material_facts: A document relating to the accounts was relied on as recording a settlement on a particular date, although it bore no party’s signature.
A family manager admitted the document’s contents and said they had been noted from account books; relevant pages of those books had been torn out.
The High Court did not properly consider the document and the manager’s admission when deciding settlement and limitation.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the document and the admission required proper consideration for determining whether there had been a full and final settlement and for determining limitation; it remitted those questions for fresh consideration without deciding whether settlement had in fact occurred.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 58 and 145 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, an admitted fact need not be proved, and a witness’s admission concerning a document or writing may be relevant when the witness’s attention has been drawn to it. The Court relied on Shreedhar Govind Kamerkar v. Yesahwant Govind Kamerkar, 2006 (14) SCALE 174, for the principle that an admitted matter need not be proved. The document’s lack of signatures, and the absence of the underlying account-book pages, did not justify disregarding the admission and document without considering their evidentiary effect.

predicates.appeal_concerning_business_accounts: The proceeding concerns a claim for accounts of a business and is before an appellate court.
predicates.document_contents_admitted: A witness accepts the contents of a document relevant to the dispute.
predicates.document_relevant_to_settlement_or_limit: The document may bear on whether accounts were finally settled or whether the claim is time-barred.

issues.definition: In an appeal concerning business accounts, an admitted document that may bear on settlement or limitation must be considered for that purpose.

issues.legal_issue: The shares of participants in an undocumented joint venture must be determined from their conduct and involvement, with joint-venture property serving as an indication of their respective interests.
material_facts: There was no written document establishing the partnership or setting out its terms and shares, and an oral partnership had not been proved.
The parties’ conduct in dealing with the business was relevant, and land associated with the enterprise had been purchased in the names of two participants.
The High Court had not adequately considered the subject matter of the venture or the extent of the participants’ shares, which required fresh determination.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the extent of the shares required specific consideration on remand, taking account of the parties’ conduct and involvement; ordinarily, the extent of each co-entrepreneur’s involvement is the criterion, and property forming part of the venture’s assets is an indication relevant to determining shares.
issues.legal_principle: Where the terms of an undocumented joint venture have not been reduced to writing, the parties’ conduct in managing the business is relevant to determining their shares, and ordinarily the extent of each participant’s involvement is the criterion. If immovable property forms part of the venture’s assets, it is an indication relevant to the determination. The Court also noted the High Court’s reliance on Section 45 of the Transfer of Property Act.

predicates.undocumented_joint_venture: The parties carried on a joint venture whose terms and allocation of shares were not recorded in a written agreement.
predicates.disputed_participant_shares: The participants’ respective interests in the venture are disputed and require determination.

issues.definition: When shares in an undocumented joint venture are disputed, they must be determined by considering the participants’ conduct and involvement.

issues.legal_issue: A court must determine whether a suit is barred by limitation even when no party has pleaded limitation.
material_facts: The suit sought accounts and other relief relating to a business, and limitation was disputed in the proceedings.
The Court considered whether the suit was time-barred and held that the issue required fresh consideration, including consideration of the relevant limitation articles and the admitted document.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the court must determine whether a suit is barred by limitation regardless of whether a party has raised that plea; it did not decide whether this suit was time-barred and remitted the question for fresh consideration.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Limitation Act requires the court to determine whether a suit is barred by limitation irrespective of whether the parties have raised the plea. The relevant limitation articles and admissible evidence bearing on limitation must be considered.

predicates.civil_suit_before_court: A court is deciding a civil suit or an appeal in which the timeliness of the suit is relevant.

issues.definition: Whenever a civil suit is before a court, the court must determine whether it is barred by limitation even if no party pleads that bar.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court must formulate appropriate points for determination and address material issues raised in the appeal; failure to do so requires fresh consideration of those issues.
material_facts: The appeal challenged a decree involving business accounts, limitation, and the participants’ respective shares.
The High Court did not adequately address the effect of the accounts document, the limitation issues, or other material points, including the extent of the claimed shares.
The Court set aside the High Court judgment in part and remitted the relevant issues for a fresh hearing with appropriate points formulated.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the High Court was required to formulate appropriate points for determination under Order XLI Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure and to consider the relevant issues afresh; it remitted the matter to the High Court.
issues.legal_principle: Order XLI Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires an appellate court to formulate appropriate points for determination. Where material issues raised in the appeal have not been addressed, the appellate court must consider them on their merits, and the judgment may be set aside to that extent and the issues remitted for fresh consideration.

predicates.appeal_from_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree.
predicates.material_issues_not_addressed: The appellate court has failed to address material issues raised in the appeal.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a decree, if material issues raised in the appeal have not been addressed, the appellate court must formulate points for determination and address those issues.
